status: DRAFT v0.1: not yet reviewed, pretested or calibrated.
notes: Uses descriptive terms ('semi-automatic rifles') rather than either side's labels. High pole is consistently 'fewer restrictions'.

items.stem: Should a background check be required when one private person sells a gun to another?
items.scope: Sales between individuals, not through a licensed dealer.
options: Yes, for every sale or transfer, including between family members
Yes, for all sales, but not gifts or loans between family and close friends
Only for sales at gun shows and online
No; private sales should not require a check

items.stem: What should the law be on semi-automatic rifles like the AR-15?
items.scope: Rifles that fire one shot per trigger pull and reload automatically, with features like a detachable magazine.
options: Ban new sales and buy back the ones people own
Ban new sales; people can keep the ones they have
Allow sales only to people 21 and older with a license and training
Allow sales with a background check, as most states do now

definitions.text: A gun that fires one round each time the trigger is pulled and loads the next round automatically. Most handguns sold today are semi-automatic.

items.stem: Should the law limit how many rounds a gun magazine can hold?
items.scope: Magazines for both handguns and rifles.
options: Yes, 10 rounds or fewer
Yes, about 15 to 20 rounds
No limit

items.stem: What should be required to carry a concealed handgun in public?
items.scope: Adults who can legally own a gun.
items.context: More than half the states now allow it without a permit.
options: Generally not allowed, except for police and security guards
A permit with training and a background check
A permit with a background check only
No permit needed

facts.source: US Concealed Carry Association; state statutes (2026)

items.stem: Should people with permits be allowed to carry guns in schools, bars and government buildings?
items.scope: Adults with a carry permit, not police.
options: No, in none of these places
Not in schools or government buildings; bars and other businesses can decide
Yes in most places, including trained teachers in schools

items.stem: Should courts be able to temporarily take guns from someone found to be a danger to themselves or others?
items.scope: Someone not convicted of a crime. Specific cases come next.
options: Yes, at the request of police or family members
Yes, at police request only, with a quick hearing where the person can respond
No; only after a criminal conviction or a formal mental health commitment

items.stem: Should a court be able to temporarily take guns from each of these people?
options: Yes
No

cases.text: Someone who posted threats of violence online but hasn't been charged
Someone a family member reports as suicidal
Someone under a temporary restraining order for domestic abuse

items.stem: What should the minimum age be to buy a gun?
items.context: Under federal law, licensed dealers can sell handguns only to people 21 and older, and rifles and shotguns to people 18 and older.
options: 21 for any gun
21 for handguns and semi-automatic rifles; 18 for hunting rifles and shotguns
21 for handguns; 18 for rifles and shotguns, as federal law requires of dealers
18 for any gun

facts.claim: 18 U.S.C. 922(b)(1): dealers may not sell handguns to under-21 or long guns to under-18

items.stem: Which comes closest to what you think the Second Amendment protects?
items.scope: Your own reading, regardless of court rulings.
options: Only the right of states to maintain militias
An individual right to own guns, subject to broad regulation
An individual right to own guns, with only narrow limits
An individual right with almost no limits
